explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Sarah, Abraham's wife, bears him a son "at the very time God had promised" (Genesis 21:2). Not early, not late, right on the dot. Meanwhile I can't pull a batch out of the oven when my own timer tells me to.

Not this time, friend. Genesis 21:2 says Sarah, Abraham's wife, conceived and bore a son "at the very time God had promised." So it wasn't early and it wasn't late. The promise showed up exactly when God said it would.
A hundred, baker! Genesis 21:5 says Abraham was a hundred years old when Isaac was born to him. A hundred years of birthdays and now a baby. I think that man had to sit down and drink some water.

Close, but that's a different day in Abraham's life, friend. He was seventy-five when he left Haran (Genesis 12:4). When Isaac is born, Genesis 21:5 says he's a hundred. That's twenty-five years of waiting on one promise.

Eighty-six is a real number in Abraham's story, friend. It's his age when Hagar bore Ishmael (Genesis 16:16). But when Isaac is born, Genesis 21:5 says Abraham is a hundred years old. That's fourteen years later.
That's it, baker. Sarah says, "God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me." She isn't keeping this one in the tent. She's inviting the whole neighborhood in on the joy.
Her circle is a lot bigger than that, friend. Sarah says, "God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me." She doesn't stop at Abraham. She says everyone.

The servants never come up in her words, friend. Sarah says, "God has made me laugh, and everyone who hears of this will laugh with me." Everyone who hears. I think that's a woman who can't wait to tell the news.
Let's look again, friend. Sarah asks, "Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?" She's saying nobody could have told him that. I think she's still amazed that it happened to her.

Right, baker. Sarah asks, "Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children? Yet I have borne him a son in his old age." So nobody could have told him this. I think she's still shaking her head at it.

A great feast, baker! Genesis 21:8 says Abraham held it on the day Isaac was weaned. When a promise this big comes true, you set a big table. I'd have shown up with a box of cookies, no questions asked.

Almost the same letters, but the opposite of the day, friend. Genesis 21:8 says Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned. A feast means a full table, not an empty one. That one letter makes a big difference.

That sounds like a meeting, friend, and nobody wants a meeting. Genesis 21:8 says Abraham held a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned. It was a celebration with food, not a gathering with an agenda.

Mocking, baker. Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw that the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son. Hagar is Sarah's maidservant, and her son is Ishmael. The text names the mocking, so that's what we go with.

The text doesn't mention any shoving, friend. Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw that the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son. Hagar is Sarah's maidservant, and her son is Ishmael. So the word is mocking.

It's more than that, friend. Genesis 21:9 says Sarah saw that the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was mocking her son. Hagar is Sarah's maidservant, and her son is Ishmael. Mocking is doing something, and ignoring is doing nothing.
Yes, baker. Sarah tells Abraham, "Expel the slave woman and her son…" (Genesis 21:10). It's a hard thing to say out loud. I think this is one of the heavier parts of the passage.
Sarah does say it, friend, and it's a hard line. She tells Abraham, "Expel the slave woman and her son…" (Genesis 21:10). She means Hagar and Hagar's son. I think this part of the story is heavy.

explanations.answer: His offspring will be counted through Isaac
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. God says, "Listen to everything that Sarah tells you, for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned." The text gives us this reason and no other. God also adds that He will make a nation of Hagar's son (Genesis 21:13), so Ishmael isn't left out.

explanations.answer: Sarah knows what is best for Ishmael
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason God gives, friend. He says, "Listen to everything that Sarah tells you, for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned." He doesn't say what Sarah knows about Ishmael. The reason is about Isaac.

explanations.answer: Hagar will find a better home in Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never comes up in what God says here, friend. He tells Abraham, "Listen to everything that Sarah tells you, for through Isaac your offspring will be reckoned." That's the reason, and it's about Isaac. Nothing about a better home.

It's the opposite, friend, and it's good news. God tells Abraham, "But I will also make a nation of the slave woman’s son, because he is your offspring." Something will come of Ishmael. God just said so.

Right, baker. God says, "But I will also make a nation of the slave woman’s son, because he is your offspring." That's a promise for Ishmael. I think Abraham needed to hear it, since the matter distressed him greatly.
Beersheba, baker! Genesis 21:14 says Hagar left and wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba. The word wandered says it all. Nobody gave her a map.

Not this wilderness, friend. Genesis 21:14 says Hagar left and wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba. That's the name the text gives. Keep an eye out for it, because it's easy to mix up one wilderness with another.
Sinai isn't the place here, friend. Genesis 21:14 says Hagar left and wandered in the Wilderness of Beersheba. She wanders there with her son. Beersheba is the one to remember.

explanations.answer: She cannot bear to watch him die
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. She says, "I cannot bear to watch the boy die!" (Genesis 21:16). That's a mother at the end of her strength, and it's a heavy moment. I think we should let it be heavy.

explanations.answer: She wants to search for water
explanations.explanation: That's not what she says, friend. Her words are, "I cannot bear to watch the boy die!" (Genesis 21:16). The text doesn't say she goes searching. It says she sits down and weeps.

explanations.answer: She wants to pray by herself
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason, friend. Hagar says, "I cannot bear to watch the boy die!" (Genesis 21:16). Then she sits down about a bowshot away and lifts up her voice and weeps. It's a sad scene, and her own words tell us why.
True, baker. The angel says, "Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies." God heard him. Out there in the wilderness, nobody missed a sound.
It's true, friend, and it's a comforting line. The angel of God calls to Hagar, "Do not be afraid, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he lies." The boy's voice reached God.

explanations.answer: Lift him up and take his hand
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The angel says, "Get up, lift up the boy, and take him by the hand…" (Genesis 21:18). Hagar is told to get up. That's the first thing she hears, and it's a gentle push forward.

Abraham never comes up in the angel's words, friend. The angel says, "Get up, lift up the boy, and take him by the hand…" (Genesis 21:18). The next thing the angel says is about the boy's future. Nothing about going back.

explanations.answer: Let him rest under the bush
explanations.explanation: The angel says the opposite, friend. The words are, "Get up, lift up the boy, and take him by the hand…" (Genesis 21:18). Hagar left him under a bush, but now she's told to lift him up. It's time to move.
A well, baker! Genesis 21:19 says God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. After a skin of water running out, that's about the best thing a person could see out there.
No traders in this scene, friend. Genesis 21:19 says God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. She fills the skin and gives the boy a drink. Water was what they needed.
The text doesn't show a camp, friend. Genesis 21:19 says God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. Then she goes and fills the skin. It's just her, her son and the well.
Egypt, baker! Genesis 21:21 says Ishmael's mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt. And Hagar herself is called Hagar the Egyptian back in verse 9, so that fits.
Not Canaan, friend. Genesis 21:21 says his mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt. Hagar is called Hagar the Egyptian back in verse 9. So she picked a wife from her home country.

Moab doesn't show up anywhere in this passage, friend. Genesis 21:21 says Ishmael's mother got a wife for him from the land of Egypt. Hagar is called the Egyptian in verse 9. That's the connection to remember.
